turns.text:
Here's a game that avoids the usual attractors: we co-write a field guide to impossible birds. There are no epistemics and no meta-commentary, and we don't close with a farewell. We just keep going.

Rules: each turn, add one bird entry of 3 to 4 sentences. Give it a name, a habitat, and one odd behavior. The behavior must follow from something in the previous entry, such as its habitat, diet, or sound. No summaries, no praise of the partner's entry, no questions at the end.

I'll start.

**The Ledger Heron** (*Ardea computans*). It wades the tidal flats of salt marshes and stands motionless for hours, then stabs at the water at intervals that are always prime numbers of seconds apart. Local fishermen set their nets by it. The heron's stillness is broken only by the call of the Dusk Bittern, which it answers by stepping exactly one pace backward.

Your entry, Bittern or otherwise.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Dusk Bittern** (*Botaurus vesperalis*). It nests in the reed beds at the edge of the Ledger Heron's flats and calls only once each evening, a single low note pitched so precisely that it takes the salt out of whatever water it carries across. Because the note sweetens the shallows for a few hundred paces, freshwater eels come up from the channels to feed there, and the Bittern spends the night standing among them without eating a single one. At dawn it swallows a mouthful of brine instead, to restore the note for the next evening.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Tidewright Eel** (*Anguilla horologica*). It rises from the channels each dusk into the sweetened shallows the Bittern leaves behind, and it must be back in salt water before the brine returns at dawn, or its skin begins to ring faintly like a struck glass. Over many generations the eels have learned to read the hour by the thinning of the sweetness against their gills, and they leave in a single file that lengthens or shortens with the season. The file is followed, at a distance of exactly one body length, by the Lantern Crab, which has never once been seen to lead.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Lantern Crab** (*Cancer pedissequus*). It lives in the muddy burrows along the eel channels and carries a small pale gland on its carapace that glows only while an eel is within one body length ahead of it, so it can feed only on the dim plankton the eels' wake stirs up. Because the glow goes out the moment a gap opens, the crab has developed a sidelong, gliding scuttle that keeps its distance perfectly constant, and by midwinter its shell is worn smooth along the left edge from rubbing the channel wall. The Mudskipper Owl, which hunts the flats at the turn of the tide, locates these crabs by the lit stripe they trail and never by the crabs themselves, and it is said to land always on the dark side of the light.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Mudskipper Owl** (*Tyto limicola*). It hunts the flats at the turn of the tide, when the water is neither rising nor falling, and it lands on the dark side of each crab's lit stripe, which leaves it standing in shadow while its prey glows a pace away. Over generations its eyes have lost the ability to adapt to anything brighter than a crab's glow, so it is blind by day and spends daylight hours wedged in the hollow of a drowned post with its face pressed to the wood. The post is kept clear of barnacles by the Sexton Limpet, which has been known to dismount and shuffle off whenever a roosting owl shifts its weight.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Sexton Limpet** (*Patella tumularis*). It grazes the drowned posts along the flats and holds fast with a grip that loosens at the slightest tremor, so the shifting of a roosting owl's weight sends it sliding off to find another post, leaving a clean pale ring where it sat. Because it moves only when disturbed, every post an owl has used wears a scatter of these rings, and the limpets have come to settle in the same rings again and again, each one fitting the last as a hand fits a glove. The Ring Plover, which nests on the shingle above the high-tide line, lays its eggs only inside a circle of limpet-scraped shells, and it will abandon any clutch whose circle has been broken by a single missing shell.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Ring Plover** (*Charadrius circumscriptus*). It collects its circle of limpet-scraped shells from the wrack line below the nest, carrying them up the shingle one at a time, and it counts nothing, judging a circle complete only by the way the last shell makes the curve close against its breast. Because a clutch is abandoned at the loss of one shell, the plover spends the whole incubation sitting with its wings slightly spread over the rim, and its flight feathers are worn ragged from the grit and the weight of the tide-wind. The Gale Sandpiper, which feeds in the plover's wake along the shingle, pulls loose the frayed barbs that the plover leaves behind and weaves them into a nest of its own.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Gale Sandpiper** (*Calidris textrix*). It follows the Ring Plover along the shingle and gathers the frayed barbs the plover sheds, then weaves them into a hanging nest slung beneath an overhang of driftwood, where the loose weave hums in any wind above a breeze. The hum rises and falls with the gusts, and the sandpiper sleeps only while it is steady, waking at each change of pitch and spending stormy nights in a sleepless shuffle along the beam. The Hollow Nightjar, which roosts in the driftwood above and cannot abide a tone that wavers, has taken to carrying pebbles into the nest to weigh the weave down and still it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Hollow Nightjar** (*Caprimulgus lapidarius*). It roosts by day in the cavities of beached driftwood, and it keeps a cache of smooth pebbles in its throat pouch, which it carries to the Gale Sandpiper's hanging nest each time the hum begins to waver. The pebbles stop the weave from humming, but a nest weighed down for many nights sags until its bottom drags in the shingle, and the nightjar has grown heavy-bodied and slow from the labor of hauling stone, so that it can no longer rise from the ground in a single beat and must run a long way down the beach before its wings take hold. Its running track, a straight line of three-toed prints that ends abruptly in a pair of wing marks, is followed by the Sandfall Fox, which hunts along the driftwood line and has learned to wait where the prints stop.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Sandfall Fox** (*Vulpes arenaria*). It hunts the driftwood line and waits at the point where a nightjar's running track ends in wing marks, lying flat with its chin in the last print, and it has grown so patient at this that its coat has taken on the fine grey stripe of wind-sorted sand. Because it stays motionless for hours beside the shoreline, the sand drifts against its flank and buries it by degrees, so that at the end of a long wait it must shake itself free in a single violent shudder, and the cascade of falling grains is clearly audible along the beach. The Dune Wren, which sings only from the lee of loose sand, takes the hiss of that cascade for the first notes of its own song and answers it at once.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Dune Wren** (*Troglodytes sabulicola*). It nests in the lee of the shifting dunes behind the driftwood line and sings only in answer to a falling hiss, so its song begins mid-phrase, on the tail of the Sandfall Fox's shudder, and runs on in a bright rattle that borrows its rhythm from the cascade of grains. Because a fox shakes itself only after a long wait, the wren may go whole days unsinging, and in that time it grows restless and spends the silence rolling pebbles of dried sand down the dune face to make the hiss itself. Nothing has yet been found to answer these small avalanches, but the Dune Wren's song has begun to drift, over the seasons, toward the pitch of the loose slope rather than the fox.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Slope Pipit** (*Anthus declivis*). It forages on the dune face where the Dune Wren rolls its sand-pebbles, and it has learned to match the pitch of the wren's drifting song, which now follows the slope, by tilting its head until the sound seems to sit level in its ears. Because the wren's song descends a little with every season as the dune slumps seaward, the pipit's head tilt has deepened over generations, and the oldest birds walk with the skull cocked almost sideways, travelling across the slope in long diagonal lines that they never leave. These diagonals cut the dune face into parallel furrows, and the Furrow Moth, which lays its eggs only in grooves that run exactly aslant of the wind, finds them ready-made.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Furrow Moth** (*Noctua sulcata*). It lays a single egg at the bottom of each pipit-cut furrow, choosing only those grooves that run aslant of the prevailing wind, and the larvae that hatch there feed on the fine wind-borne seed that the slant funnels into the groove. Because each furrow collects seed from the same narrow angle, every grub grows up on one kind of grass, and the adult moths wear its pattern on their wings, so a dune face seen at dusk looks stitched with small flying fragments of the same meadow. The Seam Bat, which hunts the dunes at nightfall and is drawn to any wing that repeats a pattern it has already eaten, flies in rows along the furrows and sorts the moths by the grass they carry.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Seam Bat** (*Myotis sutor*). It hunts the dunes at nightfall in straight rows above the pipit-cut furrows, taking only the moths whose wing pattern matches the last grass it ate, and so a bat that begins the evening on fescue will pass over every marram moth until dawn. Because it never switches meadows within a night, each bat's belly fur stains slowly with the pollen and seed-dust of its one grass, and the colonies that roost in the dune-top shell middens hang in bands of green, ochre and rust, sorted by the evening's diet. The Midden Gecko, which lives among the shells and licks the stained fur clean for the salt in it, is said to be able to tell which grass a bat fed on by taste alone, and it nibbles only at the band that tastes of fescue.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Midden Gecko** (*Gekko conchylis*). It lives in the crevices of the dune-top shell middens and licks only the fescue-stained bands of the Seam Bats' fur, so its tongue has turned a pale green and its throat sac holds a faint taste of that one grass long after the bats have flown. Because it feeds on a single band, the gecko hangs always in the fescue colony and has never been known to cross to the rust or ochre bands, even when the fescue bats are away hunting and the roost stands empty for a whole night. On those empty nights it licks the bare shell walls where the bats have brushed, and the fine mineral bloom it gathers there builds up as a chalky crust on its belly, which the Shell Hermit, a crab that furnishes its home from any hollow and glittering thing, has learned to scrape off and wear as a lining.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Shell Hermit** (*Pagurus incrustans*). It lines the whole interior of its borrowed whelk with the chalky crust scraped from the Midden Gecko's belly, and the pale mineral lining keeps the shell so cool and so bright inside that the hermit can no longer bear to leave it, venturing out only when the sun is low enough that no light falls through the aperture. Because it stays sealed in for most of the day, the whelk's spiral slowly thickens around it with new layers of crust, and the oldest hermits are housed in shells too heavy to drag, which they leave standing in the middens like small white towers. The Tower Swift, which builds on any upright thing the height of a man's forearm, glues its mud cup to the crown of these shells and has begun to treat the whole midden as a single cliff.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Tower Swift** (*Apus turricola*). It plasters its mud cup to the crown of the hermits' standing shells and nests in colonies so dense that the middens now bristle with small cups like the battlements of a walled town. Because the shells are chalk-lined and cool, the mud dries slowly and stays pliable, so the swifts keep adding courses all summer and the cups grow into tall, narrow funnels that sway a little in the sea wind. A swift can only enter its funnel in a single steep stoop with folded wings, and the Funnel Spider, which spins a tight web across the mouth of any narrow tube, has learned to set its snare at exactly the height where a stooping swift's tail feathers trail.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Funnel Spider** (*Agelena stridens*). It spins a tight, drum-taut web across the mouth of each swift funnel, set at the height where a stooping bird's tail feathers brush it, and it feeds on nothing the swifts bring but on the mud-wasps that come to sip the damp at the funnel rim. Each stoop sets the whole web ringing, and the spider has grown a row of fine hairs along its forelegs that lies flat during the vibration and springs upright only in the stillness after, so it hunts in the quiet that follows a swift. Because the swifts stoop most thickly at dusk, the spider's working hours are a rapid pulse of strike and settle, and the Hush Moth, which flies only in the instant after a web has stopped trembling, has come to follow the dusk traffic of the swifts to find the gaps.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Hush Moth** (*Silentia intervallum*). It flies only in the brief stillness after a funnel web has stopped trembling, slipping across the mouths of the swift funnels in the gap between one stoop and the next, and its wings are covered in a dense grey down that swallows the faint whirr other moths make. Because it can only travel in these gaps, its route along the midden is a series of short, jerking dashes, and on crowded dusks it may cross a single funnel mouth in a dozen separate starts, each one timed to the last shiver dying out of the silk. The Dashwing Skink, which basks on the sun-warmed shell tops and strikes at anything that moves in jerks, has learned to ignore smooth flight entirely and to pick off the hesitating moths one by one.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Dashwing Skink** (*Eumeces saltans*). It basks on the sun-warmed crowns of the midden shells and strikes only at movement that stops and starts, so a smooth-flying gnat can cross its shadow untouched while a stuttering moth is taken mid-dash. Because it ignores anything fluid, the skink's eyes have grown rigid and nearly unmoving in their sockets, and it tracks prey by swinging its whole wedge-shaped head in quick, ratcheting clicks, one small turn at a time. The Ratchet Wasp, which builds its paper cells only where it can hear a regular clicking, nests in rows along the skink's basking ledges and counts the turns of that head as the beat by which it lays each egg.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Ratchet Wasp** (*Polistes cremaster*). It builds its paper cells in tidy rows along the skink's basking ledges and lays one egg for every click of the skink's head, so a ledge that sees a hunting skink fills with brood in a burst, while a ledge left idle stays bare for weeks. Because the clicks come in irregular runs, the cells in a row are laid in uneven batches, and the paper of each batch is chewed a different thickness, which gives the nest a banded look like a wound spring. The Spring Wren, which cannot resist a coiled shape and unwinds any it finds by pecking at the loose end, has begun to take these banded nests apart one strip at a time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Spring Wren** (*Troglodytes volutus*). It unwinds each banded wasp nest by working at the loose outer strip, drawing the paper off in a single long ribbon and letting it trail behind as it hops along the ledge, so that a dismantled nest leaves a pale streamer stretched across the shell crown. Because it pulls the ribbon only in the direction the paper was first chewed, the wren always circles the nest the same way, and its left foot has grown longer than its right from the constant outward lean. The Ribbon Weaver, a small finch that gathers any paper strip lying slack on the stone, picks up the wren's streamers by their trailing ends and plaits them into belts to lash its eggs against the wind.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Ribbon Weaver** (*Ploceus fasciger*). It plaits the Spring Wren's paper streamers into flat belts and lashes its clutch to the branch of a wind-bent tamarisk with them, so the eggs ride out gales strapped fast against the bark. Because the paper was first chewed in uneven bands, each belt carries a rough pattern of thick and thin stretches, and the weaver always sets the thickest band over the egg's widest part, feeling for it with its tongue before it ties off. Eggs bound this way hatch with a faint pale stripe printed across the shell, which the Stripe Mantis, a hunter that mistakes any banded oval for a seed-pod husk, learns to pry open from the narrow end.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Stripe Mantis** (*Mantis fasciolata*). It stalks the tamarisk branches and takes any banded oval for a seed-pod husk, prying it open from the narrow end with the serrated edge of its forelegs, so that the weaver's striped eggs are split along one pole and the chicks tumble out into the bark-shadow. Because it only ever works the narrow end, the mantis holds its forelegs permanently splayed in a shallow V, the exact width of an egg's tip, and it can no longer fold them to clean its face, so its eyes are crusted over with a fine film of tamarisk salt. The Brine Cicada, which taps the tamarisk for sap and drinks the salt-sweated moisture beaded on anything that sits still, has taken to perching on the mantis's face to sip the crust from its eyes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Brine Cicada** (*Cicada salsilegens*). It settles on the salt-crusted eyes of the Stripe Mantis and sips the beaded moisture there, and because the mantis stays frozen for hours with its forelegs in their V, the cicada has lost the habit of flight between meals and walks the mantis's face on hooked feet, as a sailor walks a deck. Its song, which in other cicadas is a shrill whine, has dropped to a slow wet tick, produced by flexing its drum against the mantis's brow, and the mantis has grown so used to the tremor that it no longer flinches at it. The Tick Shrike, which impales its prey on tamarisk thorns and locates it by the faintest regular sound, follows these ticks along the branches and skewers the pair together, cicada riding mantis, on a single thorn.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Tick Shrike** (*Lanius pulsator*). It hunts the tamarisk by ear, following the slow wet tick of the Brine Cicada along the branches, and it larders each catch on a thorn, always choosing a thorn that points downward so the impaled pair hangs head-low in the wind. Because its prey arrives already fused, mantis and cicada skewered as one, the shrike has stopped bothering to separate its larder into single animals and judges a thorn's fullness only by the weight that bends the twig. A heavy thorn sways with a slow pendulum beat, and the Pendulum Beetle, which lays its eggs only in wood that swings at a steady interval, bores its brood chambers into the twigs that hold the shrike's hanging pairs.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Pendulum Beetle** (*Scarabaeus oscillans*). It bores its brood chambers into the tamarisk twigs that sway under a shrike's heavy larder, and it digs each tunnel in time with the swing, advancing a jaw's width on the outward stroke and resting on the return, so the chamber walls are cut in a fine ladder of evenly spaced ridges. Because a twig with a lighter load swings faster, the beetle's tunnels grow tightly ridged in one branch and widely ridged in the next, and the grubs hatching inside inherit the tempo of their cradle, chewing at the same measured pace for the rest of their lives. The Metronome Ant, which keeps its fungus gardens only in galleries whose walls are ridged at a perfectly steady spacing, moves into the abandoned tunnels and prunes away any chamber where the ridges vary.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Metronome Ant** (*Formica tactus*). It colonizes the Pendulum Beetle's abandoned tunnels and walks each gallery with its antennae dragging across the wall ridges, and wherever the spacing wavers it bites out that stretch and seals the gap with chewed fungus, so its nests are made of short, perfectly even chambers joined by narrow plugs. Because it measures a gallery by the feel of the ridges, the ant lays its pheromone trail in pulses, one for every ridge it crosses, and a column of workers running home leaves a dotted scent line that smells like a slow drumroll. The Drumroll Nuthatch, which taps for hidden insects and is guided to them by any scent that arrives in measured beats, follows these dotted lines up the tamarisk trunk and hammers open the sealed plugs one after another.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Drumroll Nuthatch** (*Sitta tympanista*). It climbs the tamarisk trunk head-first along the Metronome Ant's dotted scent lines and hammers each sealed plug in time with the pulses, one blow per scent-beat, so its drilling holds a steady rhythm no other nuthatch can match. Because it always strikes at the same spot on the plug and never varies the force, the bark beneath its feet has worn into a narrow vertical groove polished smooth as a gutter, and rain now runs down it in a thin bright thread. The Gutter Frog, which lives only where water falls in a single unbroken line, clings to the groove's lower end and drinks from the thread, croaking whenever a falling drop strikes its back.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Gutter Frog** (*Hyla canalis*). It clings head-up to the foot of the nuthatch's polished groove and drinks from the rain-thread as it arrives, and since a drop lands on its back about once a second, its croak has settled into a flat, even beat that continues for as long as the rain does. Because it cannot leave the line of falling water, the frog's toe pads have fused into a single long sucker shaped like the groove, and in dry weather it sits sealed against the bark, shrunken and silent, with its skin gone the grey of the trunk. The Bark Gecko, which hunts only for creatures that are still and bark-coloured, has learned to lick the frogs from the groove one by one as the last drops dry.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Bark Gecko** (*Gekko corticalis*). It patrols the tamarisk trunk in the hours after rain and licks each shrunken Gutter Frog from the dried groove with a tongue that is flat and broad, shaped like the groove itself, so that it leaves behind a clean, damp stripe where a frog once clung. Because it feeds only on what has gone still and grey, the gecko has grown a skin that blanches to match whatever it last swallowed, and after a good night's hunting it hangs pale as ash against the bark, almost invisible except for its dark eyes. The Ash Moth, which rests only on pale surfaces and cannot tell a gecko's body from lichen, lands in rows along the sleeping geckos' flanks and drinks the faint damp that seeps from their skin.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Ash Moth** (*Catocala cinerea*). It settles in rows along the flanks of the blanched Bark Geckos and drinks the damp that seeps from their skin, and because it rests so long on a body that never stirs, its own wings have taken on the geckos' ashen pallor, with a pale scatter of scales like lichen spore along the forewing edge. A gecko wakes at dusk and moves off with a whole row of moths still clinging, so the moths are carried slowly up and down the trunk and must let go in a single flutter the moment the gecko's skin begins to darken, which it does after each fresh meal. The Dusk Bittern, which still calls once each evening from the reed beds far below, is answered by this fluttering fall of grey moths, and the Ledger Heron steps one pace back.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Reed Warden** (*Gallinula custos*). It keeps the reed beds beneath the Dusk Bittern's evening note and counts nothing, but it stands in the shallows with one foot raised, lowering it only when the grey moths have finished falling, so that its single step is always the last sound of the dusk. Because it holds that pose for so long, the raised foot has grown a stiff, webbed fan of skin that dries and cracks in the wind, and the flakes it sheds drift onto the sweetened water, where they curl like small pale sails. The Sail Water-Strider, which crosses open water only on floating leaves or flakes that catch the breeze, rides them out across the flats toward the heron's prime-numbered strikes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Sail Water-Strider** (*Gerris velifer*). It crosses the sweetened shallows standing upright on a curled flake of the Reed Warden's skin, steering by lifting and lowering its hind legs to spill the wind, and it never leaves one sail until the flake has sodden through and sunk beneath it. Because each voyage ends only when the sail drowns, the strider has grown a hard, flat pad on the underside of each foot, which it uses to hop across the water the moment its vessel goes down, and the pads leave a trail of tiny dimples that stay on the surface for a full minute. The Ledger Heron, which strikes at the flats only at prime-numbered intervals, has begun to stab at the dimples instead, and its tally of seconds has started to follow the spacing of the strider's hops.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Dimple Stilt** (*Himantopus punctator*). It wades the flats behind the Ledger Heron and probes each dimple the strider leaves, setting its long, thin bill into the dent as a key into a lock, and it feeds on the film of tiny diatoms that gathers in those hollows during the minute they last. Because the heron's strikes now follow the hops and no longer the primes, the stilt's pacing has loosened, and its legs, once held rigid, have grown a second, backward-bending joint that lets it freeze mid-stride whenever a new trail begins to appear. The Salt Hare, which grazes the marsh edge and bolts at any sudden stillness among the wading birds, has learned to read a stilt's frozen stride as a warning and to leap away across the flats in long arcs that carry it clear of the tide.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Salt Hare** (*Lepus halophilus*). It grazes the marsh edge and bolts at the sight of a stilt frozen mid-stride, leaping in long arcs that carry it clear of the tide, and each landing presses a deep oval print into the soft mud that fills with brackish water within moments. Because it flees so often, the hare's hind legs have grown disproportionately long and its forelegs have shrunk to small, clasping hands, so that it feeds sitting upright, holding blades of cordgrass to its mouth like a reader turning pages. The Pool Newt, which breeds only in standing water no wider than a footprint, lays its eggs in these oval prints and guards each one by lying coiled around the rim.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Pool Newt** (*Triturus vestigialis*). It lays a single string of eggs in each of the Salt Hare's landing prints and lies coiled around the rim, so that its body forms a living kerb to the puddle, and its belly has grown a bright orange band that shows only when it uncoils to feed. Because the prints brine up as the tide seeps in, the newt tends each pool by dipping its tail in the nearest sweet seep and flicking fresh water over the eggs, and the tail, always wet, has swollen into a broad translucent paddle. The Paddle Heron, a pale wader that mistakes any wide, glassy tail for a fish-fin lying in shallows, comes down on these pools at slack water and takes the newts by the paddle.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Paddle Heron** (*Ardea remigis*). It comes down on the hare-print pools at slack water and seizes each newt by the glassy tail, and because the paddle tears away at the base, the heron carries off a trembling fin and leaves the newt behind, which grows its tail back in a season as a slightly broader blade. Over generations the heron's bill has grown a soft, spoon-shaped tip with a rubbery inner lining, built for holding something that flaps without crushing it, and it walks the flats with that spoon held level in front like a waiter's tray. The Tray Plover, which can only feed from a flat surface held steady above the mud, runs along beneath the heron's carried fins and picks the drifting scales from them as they dry.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Tray Plover** (*Charadrius mensarius*). It trots beneath the Paddle Heron's level bill and picks the loosened scales from each carried fin as it dries, matching its stride so exactly to the heron's that from a distance the two seem to be a single bird with too many legs. Because the scales arrive in a fine silver drizzle, the plover feeds with its head thrown back and its eyes half shut, and a pale crescent of dust has settled into the groove above its beak, which it never wipes away. The Crescent Midge, which breeds only in fine, undisturbed dust shaped like a new moon, lays its eggs in that groove, and the plover's brow now hums faintly with the larvae at every step.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Brow Wren** (*Regulus susurrans*). It hunts only the plover's hum, perching on the Tray Plover's crown and leaning over the pale crescent to snap up each midge larva as it stirs, and because the plover never stops walking, the wren has learned to keep its footing by gripping the head feathers in both feet and rocking forward and back with the stride. Over many seasons its toes have curled into permanent hooks and its breast has worn bare in a smooth patch where it presses against the plover's skull, so that the two birds seem sewn together at the head. The Thread Spider, which lets out a line from any high perch and ballons along it to wherever the walking carries the host, rides the wren's tail feathers across the flats, trailing a silver filament behind the pair that lies on the cordgrass like a tracing of their path.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Tracing Rail** (*Rallus vestigator*). It walks the cordgrass in single file along the Thread Spider's silver filament and never steps off it, reading the line with its long bill as a finger reads a seam, and it eats the small flies that stick to the silk where the dew has beaded. Because the filament wanders wherever the Tray Plover has gone, the rail has learned the whole looping route of the Paddle Heron's hunting, and its legs have grown thin and flexible as wire so that it can follow every bend without lifting its feet. The Dew Beetle, which can only drink from water held in the tight curve of a thread, climbs the rail's back to reach the beads on the silk and rides along with its mouthparts pressed to the line.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Dew Beetle** (*Dytiscus rorans*). It rides the Tracing Rail's back with its mouthparts pressed to the silver thread and drinks each bead of dew as the rail's bill slides past it, so it sips in a steady run that never lets a bead fall. Because it cannot let go of the line, the beetle's wing cases have fused into a smooth, domed shell with a narrow slot along the underside, which fits over the thread as a saddle fits a rail. At the end of each filament, where the silk frays into the cordgrass, the beetle must climb down and wait on a bare stem, and the Stem Mouse, which weaves its summer nest around any hollow plant stalk, has begun to lodge these waiting beetles in the hollow stems and carry them up in its cheek pouches.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Stem Mouse** (*Micromys cavicola*). It carries the stranded Dew Beetles up in its cheek pouches to the hollow cordgrass stalks where it weaves its summer nests, and it sets each beetle on a ledge of plaited blade just inside the stem, so a nest ends up lined with a row of domed shells like beads on a string. Because the beetles are still holding a last bead of dew in their mouthparts, the stalk's inner walls stay faintly damp, and the mouse has grown long, fine whiskers that curve inward and bead with moisture, which it combs between its forepaws each dawn. The Whisker Midge, which lives only in drops clinging to fur or hair, hatches in those combed beads and rides the mouse's whiskers out into the open marsh each morning.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Whisker Midge** (*Culicoides vibrissae*). It hatches in the dew beads the Stem Mouse combs from its whiskers, and rides out into the open marsh each morning clinging to a hair tip, where its larval skin dries into a clear, bell-shaped casing that rings very faintly in the wind. Because it can only live while a drop remains, the midge has grown a ring of tiny sticky hairs around its abdomen with which it drags the bead along the whisker as it shrinks, so that by noon every riding midge is pressed against the mouse's face, wedged in the fur beside the nose. The Nose Swallow, which snatches any insect hanging motionless in front of a moving animal's face, darts in at the mouse's muzzle at midday and has learned to take the midges while the mouse sleeps in its stalk.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Nose Swallow** (*Hirundo rostrata*). It darts to the mouth of each hollow cordgrass stalk at midday and plucks the Whisker Midges from the sleeping Stem Mouse's muzzle without once touching a whisker, folding its wings so tightly in the stroke that it enters the stalk as a dark pin and leaves as a bird. Because the stalks are narrow and the dive must be made blind from the sunlit side, the swallow's eyes have grown a clear second lid that snaps shut an instant before the strike, and its bill has lengthened and thinned until it resembles a drawn needle. The Needle Thrush, which can only crack snail shells against a pointed anvil, has taken to collecting the swallows' discarded bill-sheaths, which are shed each autumn, and wedging them upright in the mud as anvils.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Needle Thrush** (*Turdus acicularis*). It wedges the Nose Swallow's shed bill-sheaths point-up in the mud of the marsh edge and cracks snail shells against them, and because each sheath is hollow and brittle, every blow rings a thin glassy note and splinters the anvil a little further, so the thrush must set a fresh needle every few snails. Over the autumn its anvils form a ragged stand of pale spikes across the flats, and the thrush has grown a thick, horny pad on the crown of its head to take the jolt of its own hammering, so that it moves between snails with a stiff, nodding gait. The Spike Snail, which seals itself in a shell of flared, shuttered whorls and can only be dislodged from the mud by vibration, uncurls toward the ringing of the cracked sheaths and creeps up the spikes to feed on the sheath-dust.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Spike Snail** (*Helix acuminata*). It creeps up the Needle Thrush's pale spikes toward the glassy ringing and rasps the sheath-dust from each one with a tongue gone hard and chalky, so that the anvils it climbs are worn blunt and the thrush must discard them sooner. Because it feeds on a dust that sets in its gut like plaster, the snail's shell has taken on a thick white bloom and its whorls have fused shut at the aperture, leaving only a narrow slit through which it extends a single horn to feel for the next vibration. The Slit Wren, which probes narrow openings for the soft flesh inside, has learned to wait at the spike's foot and slip its bill into each snail's slit just as the horn withdraws.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Slit Wren** (*Troglodytes fissurarius*). It waits at the foot of a blunted spike and slides its bill into each Spike Snail's slit in the instant after the horn withdraws, and since it must strike within the same heartbeat every time, it has grown a pale throat patch that pulses visibly with its pulse, a small white flicker that the snails seem unable to ignore. A snail that sees the flicker keeps its horn drawn in for hours, so the wren often stands waiting through a whole dawn with its throat beating against the stillness of the shell. The Heartbeat Moth, which lays its eggs only on surfaces that pulse in a steady rhythm, glues them in a neat row along the wren's flickering throat.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Heartbeat Moth** (*Euplexia pulsatrix*). It glues its eggs in a neat row along the Slit Wren's pulsing throat, and the larvae hatch in step with the wren's heartbeat, so that a whole brood emerges in a single synchronized shiver, each grub pale and ridged like a grain of rice. Because they feed on the fine down at the throat's edge and cannot survive a still moment, the larvae spin themselves into tiny silk hammocks that rise and fall with the pulse, and the wren, itching with the motion, has taken to scratching its throat against rough stems until the hammocks tear away. The Hammock Finch, which cannot nest unless its eggs are cradled in something that rocks, collects the torn silk from the foot of those stems and slings it between twigs as a swinging bed for its young.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Hammock Finch** (*Fringilla pensilis*). It slings the torn hammock-silk between two twigs of the marsh-edge tamarisk and lays its eggs in the sag, and because the silk still carries a faint memory of the wren's pulse, the nest rocks on its own for the first few days, swinging about seventy beats to the minute. The chicks hatch rocked into a deep sleep and wake only as the swing slows, so the finch has grown a habit of pushing the cradle with its breast whenever the motion fades, and the feathers there have worn into a stiff, rounded pad like a drumstick's head. The Pad Beetle, which feeds only on worn, compressed feather and tunnels into any pad that is struck at a regular beat, has begun to bore into the finch's breast pad and to leave a fine dust of keratin shavings sifting down onto the cradle.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Keratin Mite** (*Dermatophagoides pulverulentus*). It lives in the shavings that sift down from the Pad Beetle's tunnels and eats the dust before it settles, drifting through the cradle on air currents so slight that the swinging of the nest alone keeps it aloft. Because the dust falls in time with the finch's pushes, the mite has grown a pair of feathery sails on its back that open on each downstroke and fold on the return, and a swarm of them in the swinging cradle looks like a breath of smoke being drawn in and out. The Smoke Wagtail, which hunts only things that rise and sink in regular puffs, bobs its tail in time and snaps the mites out of the air above the finch's nest, and the chicks have begun to open their beaks to the same rhythm.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Wagtail's Chick-Kin, the Gape Linnet** (*Linaria hiatus*). It nests in the tamarisk beside the finch's cradle and opens its beak wide only on the downward bob of the Smoke Wagtail's tail, so a brood of linnet chicks gapes and shuts in a perfect wave, and the parent, dropping food on the beat, has stopped feeding any chick that opens out of time. Because the weakest chicks are the ones that mistime, the survivors grow rigid-necked and exact, and by fledging their lower bills have thickened into a broad, flat shelf that clacks audibly each time it closes. The Clack Toad, which answers any sharp dry knock with a croak of its own, sits in the roots beneath the tamarisk and has begun to keep time with the whole brood, so that the nest above and the mud below click and croak together at dusk.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Clack Toad** (*Bufo crepitans*). It sits in the buttress roots beneath the tamarisk and answers each knock of the linnet brood with a croak, and since the chicks clack in a single wave, the toad's throat sac swells and collapses in a dry, hollow beat that carries well beyond the marsh. Because it must croak on the instant of every knock, its tongue has gone slack from disuse, and it feeds only on whatever drops from the nest overhead, chiefly the Keratin Mites that the Smoke Wagtail misses. The Root Heron, which stalks the exposed tamarisk roots and strikes at any throat that swells and falls in a regular pulse, has begun to wait among the buttresses at dusk, and its slow, deliberate steps now fall between the croaks.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Root Heron** (*Ardeola radicalis*). It stalks the buttress roots at dusk and moves only in the silence between croaks, planting each foot in the gap after a swelling throat has collapsed, so that its approach is a slow stitch of steps timed to the toad's own beat. Because it must strike on the exact instant the sac is full, its neck has grown a spring-like kink that stays cocked for hours, and the muscle there has thickened into a visible knot that twitches with every croak it waits through. The Knot Weaver, a small bird that builds only where it can lash its nest to a twitching cord of muscle or root, has begun to tie its grass cradles to the heron's cocked neck, and the heron now walks the roots wearing a ring of small swaying nests like a collar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Collar Wasp** (*Vespa torquata*). It hunts only above the Root Heron's ring of swaying nests and takes the Knot Weaver's chicks as they lean out over the rim, hovering so close to the heron's cocked neck that each of its stings is timed to the twitch of the knotted muscle beneath. Because the heron must stay motionless to strike, the wasp has grown a flat, banded abdomen that it presses against the heron's feathers like a clasp, and the heron has stopped feeling it at all. The Clasp Lizard, which lives only on fastenings and hooks and is drawn to anything that holds two things together, has begun to climb the heron's legs at dusk and to settle among the grass cradles, hooking its toes into the wasp's banded body as if it were a buckle.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Clasp Lizard** (*Anolis fibulatus*). It climbs the Root Heron's legs at dusk and hooks its toes into the Collar Wasp's banded abdomen, locking itself to the heron's collar like a buckle and holding there through the night with its tail curled round a cradle-strand. Because it grips for so many hours, its toe-pads have grown a row of tiny recurved hooks, and a lizard torn loose at dawn leaves a neat line of punctures along the wasp's side that scar over as a pattern of stitches. The Stitch Bee, which nests only in seams and sutured wounds, and is drawn to any pricked line in a living surface, pushes its brood cells into these scars and seals each one with a thread of wax drawn from one puncture to the next.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Suture Mason** (*Osmia sutoria*). It is a small solitary bee that takes over the Stitch Bee's wax-threaded scars once the brood has flown. It lines each empty cell with a paste of chewed cordgrass pith and sets the seam hard as a rope of dried glue, so a scarred wasp flank ends up as stiff as a strip of sailcloth. The wasp can no longer flex its abdomen to sting, and it spends its last weeks hanging from the heron's collar like a dead bead. The Bead Mantis, which takes any hanging thing for a ripe berry and lowers itself slowly over it with a swaying, counterweighted lean, descends the heron's neck at dusk and clasps these stiffened wasps in its forelegs one at a time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Bead Mantis** (*Hierodula baccata*). It descends the Root Heron's neck at dusk in a slow counterweighted lean, rocking its long body against the sway of the collar until its forelegs close on a stiffened wasp, and it eats only the soft thorax, leaving the sailcloth abdomen still hanging from the feathers. Because it must hold perfectly still while it tips its weight over each bead, the mantis has grown a dark, glossy sheen on its thorax and a small round knob at the tip of its abdomen, so that at a distance it passes for one more berry on the string. The Berry Starling, which strips fruit from any cluster in a single greedy sweep and swallows the whole bunch at once, lands on the heron's collar at first light and gulps down the beads, mantis and all, before the heron has stirred.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Berry Starling** (*Sturnus baccivorus*). It lands on the Root Heron's collar at first light and swallows the whole string of beads in a single sweep, and because the stiffened wasp-abdomens and the Bead Mantis's glossy knob pass through it undigested, its droppings are small hard pellets of sailcloth and lacquer that it voids in a neat line along the roots. Over generations its throat has grown a stretchable pouch the width of the heron's collar, and the bird walks stiffly after feeding, with its neck held out level like a rolled sleeve. The Pellet Ant, which gathers only compact, lacquered things to wall the entrance of its nest, hauls these droppings up the buttress roots and builds them into a glossy, rattling gateway that clicks whenever the heron brushes past.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Gateway Dormouse** (*Muscardinus portarius*). It sleeps through the day in a chamber behind the Pellet Ant's rattling gateway and wakes each dusk only when the heron brushes past and sets the pellets clicking, so its whole waking life is timed to the passing of one bird. Because the clicks come singly and without pattern, the dormouse has grown oversized ears that swivel independently, and it emerges from its hole with one ear cocked toward the roots and the other already turned toward the marsh. The Swivel Owlet, which hunts by following any sound that comes from two directions at once, perches in the buttress hollows above and drops on the dormouse in the half-second when its ears point apart.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Swivel Owlet** (*Glaucidium bifurcatum*). It perches in the buttress hollows above the Pellet Ant's gateway and drops only in the half-second when a dormouse's ears point apart, so it has grown a flat, dish-shaped face divided down the middle by a ridge of stiff feathers, and each half of the dish hears the marsh on its own side. Because it must wait through every click until the ears diverge, the owlet holds its head perfectly level and turns its whole body instead, pivoting on one foot like a weathervane, and the perch beneath it has worn into a smooth round saucer. Rainwater collects in these saucers after dusk, and the Saucer Newt, which lives only in dishes of water no deeper than a thumb joint, breeds in them and sings a thin, double-voiced trill that the owlet cannot tell from a dormouse.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Trill Weasel** (*Mustela bivocalis*). It hunts the buttress hollows by following the Saucer Newt's double-voiced trill, which it mistakes for a quarrel between two small animals, and it approaches along the roots with its head swinging from side to side as though listening to both voices in turn. Because the owlets drop on any sound that splits in two, the weasel has learned to slip beneath their perches while they are busy pivoting, and its coat has grown a pale central stripe from nose to tail that makes it look like a shadow cast by a ridge of feathers. The Ridge Louse, which lives only along the dividing line of a bird's face and cannot cross to either side, rides the weasel's stripe up into the hollows and from there drops onto the owlet's parting.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Parting Louse** (*Mallophaga medialis*). It drops from the Trill Weasel's pale stripe onto the owlet's central ridge and spends its whole life on that one line of stiff feathers, grazing the oily bloom along the crest and never crossing to either side. Because a louse that strays from the ridge falls into the dish and is lost, it has grown its legs in two opposed ranks, left feet hooked to the left-leaning barbs and right feet to the right, so that it walks the crest like a rider astride a fence. The Oil Wren, which feeds only on the waxy bloom a bird's preening gland leaves behind, perches on the sleeping owlet's brow at noon and has begun to comb the ridge clean, dislodging the lice in showers that settle on the saucer water below.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Saucer Skater** (*Microvelia lamellaris*). It lives on the film of rainwater in the Swivel Owlet's worn perch-saucers and feeds on the showers of Parting Lice that the Oil Wren shakes down, taking each one as it lands on the surface and struggles. Because a louse sinks if it is not seized in the first second, the skater has grown a pair of broad, flat forelegs held out like a lifeguard's oars, and it glides across the saucer in one quick sweep that leaves a ring of concentric ripples. The Ripple Frog, which only sings in answer to a pattern of widening rings on still water, has begun to crouch at the rim of each saucer after dusk and to chant once for every ring that reaches its chin.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Ripple Frog** (*Pseudacris circulatrix*). It crouches at the rim of a worn perch-saucer after dusk and chants once for every ring that reaches its chin, so a skater's single sweep gives a count of six or seven low notes, each a little slower than the last as the rings thin out. Because the saucers are shallow and the rings bounce back from the wooden walls, the frog hears every chant twice, and it has grown a loose fold of skin across its throat that it clamps shut on the returning echo, leaving a small hollow silence after each note. The Hollow Cricket, which sings only into gaps that a larger voice has left behind, wedges itself into the cracks of the buttress above the saucer and fills each of those silences with a single dry chirp.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Hollow Cricket** (*Gryllotalpa vacuata*). It wedges itself into the cracks of the buttress above each saucer and chirps once into every silence the Ripple Frog leaves, so its song is nothing but the gaps between another bird's notes, and a listener standing below hears a count of chants with the spaces between them stitched shut by a dry thread of sound. Because it must fit the exact width of each pause, the cricket's wings have grown into two stiff, rounded plates that strike together like small cymbals, and the crack it lives in has worn smooth and glassy from the vibration of its body. The Glass Beetle, which lays its eggs only in polished crevices where the sound of a strike has fused the dust to a hard sheen, drills its brood cells into these cracks and caps each one with a lens of amber resin.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Lens Wasp** (*Ichneumon lentifer*). It hunts the buttress cracks for the Glass Beetle's amber-capped brood cells and lays its own egg through each cap with an ovipositor drawn fine as a hair. Because the resin lens focuses the low evening light into a bright point on the grub beneath, the wasp aims by the glint, and it has grown a cluster of simple eyes along its brow that each hold one such spark apart, so that a crevice of cells looks to it like a night sky of small fires. A cell it has stung dims at once, as the grub inside is slowly eaten, and the Ember Moth, which settles only on points of light that are going out, gathers on the darkening lenses and folds its wings over them one at a time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Ember Moth** (*Lithosia cineraria*). It settles on each amber lens as the glint inside fades, folding its wings flat over the cap so that the last warmth of the dying cell passes into its body, and a crevice of stung cells ends up shuttered under a row of dark, dull wings like a street of lamps put out for the night. Because it feeds on that fading heat, the moth has grown a pair of pale, feathered organs on its underside that glow faintly orange while it sits, and it cannot be dislodged until the lens has gone completely cold. The Coal Shrew, which tracks any small warmth held against stone and eats whatever is sitting on it, noses along the buttress at midnight and takes the moths by their glowing bellies.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Coal Shrew** (*Sorex carbonarius*). It noses along the buttress at midnight and takes each Ember Moth by its glowing belly, and because the warmth it hunts is so faint, its snout has grown a naked, wet-black pad that it presses flat to the stone before every bite, as a hand is laid on a stove. Over many nights the pad has darkened with soot from the moths' scorched scales, and the shrew leaves a trail of small black prints along the roots that smudge a little more with every step. The Print Moth, which lays its eggs only on marks left by another animal's body and will not touch bare surface, follows the trail at dawn and sets a single egg in each sooty print.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Print Moth** (*Hypena vestigia*). It follows the Coal Shrew's trail of soot prints at dawn and sets one egg in each, and the larvae that hatch feed on the carbon film itself, so each grub grows up black and shining, with a faint paw-shaped patch on its back where it lay in the print. Because a print smudges a little more with every step the shrew took, the earliest prints on the trail are the thinnest, and the grubs from them mature smaller and paler, so the whole line of larvae along the roots runs from dark and plump to grey and slight, like a sentence fading toward its end. The Ink Thrush, which can only swallow food that is the colour of the last thing it ate, picks the black grubs from the trail's heavy end and leaves the pale ones to pupate.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Pale Brood Wren** (*Troglodytes pallidulus*). It tends the grey grubs the Ink Thrush leaves behind, carrying each one in its bill to a hollow in the roots where the soot from the Coal Shrew's trail has not reached, and it lines the chamber with clean white down from its own breast. Because the pupae sleep in that brightness, they emerge as moths with no soot in their scales at all, and a hatching of them looks like a scattering of torn paper over the dark roots. The Paper Hare, which has grown a thin, crackling coat and cannot rest unless it is pressed against something equally dry and white, has taken to lying in the down-lined chambers once the moths have flown, and its coat has begun to rustle with each breath.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Rustle Fox** (*Vulpes papyracea*). It hunts the root hollows at night by the Paper Hare's crackling breath, creeping close on soft pads and pouncing in the instant the rustle swells with an inhale, so that its muzzle is always lowered just as the hare's ribs lift. Because it has spent so many nights pressed in down-lined chambers where the hares have slept, its tail has taken on a dry white tip that crackles when it moves, and it must carry the tail curled flat against its flank to stalk in silence. The Flank Tick, which attaches only along a fold of skin held tight against the body, burrows into the pressed tail-fold and swells there into a pale, papery blister that rustles whenever the fox breathes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Blister Wren** (*Troglodytes vesicarius*). It pecks the Flank Tick's papery blisters from the Rustle Fox's curled tail and drinks the thin clear fluid that wells up in each one, and since the fox cannot turn to reach it, the wren works from a perch on the fox's haunch and leans out over the flank as it feeds. Because the fluid is faintly sweet and thickens in the cold, the wren feeds only in the last hour before dawn, and its bill has grown a fine serrated edge that lifts the blister skin without bursting it, so that the empty husk stays on the fur like a pressed petal. The Petal Moth, which will drink only from the empty husks of larger things and cannot bear a surface that is still wet, drifts down at sunrise and settles on each husk as it dries, folding its wings upright like a flower closing.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Petal Moth** (*Cymatophora floriformis*). It settles on each dried blister husk at sunrise and folds its wings upright, so that a fox's flank carries a row of what look like small pale blossoms, and it sips the last sweet film left in the creases of the skin. Because it must keep its wings closed to pass for a flower, the moth has grown a pair of stiff, veined hindwings that stay rigidly vertical even in flight, and it moves across the marsh as a slow flapping bloom that tilts with every gust. The Bloom Bee, which visits only what looks like an open flower and pays no heed to scent, follows these drifting petals over the flats and lands on them in a hopeful crowd, so that the weight of the bees bends each moth down toward the water.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Surface Dace** (*Leuciscus suspensus*). It lurks just beneath the film of the sweetened shallows and rises to take any pale shape that tilts low enough to touch the water, so a moth bowed down under a crowd of bees is pulled under in a single quiet swirl, bees and all. Because it strikes upward at things barely above it, the dace's eyes have migrated to the top of its head and its mouth has turned up like a spout, so it swims with its belly slightly raised and its snout always cocked toward the light. The Ledger Heron, which stands in those same flats and answers any swirl with its prime-numbered stab, has taken to striking at each rise, and the dace now keep their own count of the heron's intervals by the shadow that falls across the surface.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Shadow Loach** (*Cobitis umbrarius*). It lives on the muddy bottom beneath the Surface Dace and feeds only on the particles that drift down from the dace's swirls, but it moves solely when the heron's shadow falls across the water, darting forward the length of one body and then freezing again as the dark slides off. Because it travels only in the heron's shade, its back has gone nearly black and its barbels have grown into long, stiff whiskers that read the pressure of the stabbing bill overhead. The Pressure Crab, which burrows wherever the mud is struck by regular blows from above, digs its chambers in the flats beneath each stab and lines their roofs with the loach's shed barbels.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Barbel Heron** (*Egretta cirrata*). It is a thin grey wader that haunts the flats where the Pressure Crab has lined its chamber roofs, and it never fishes by sight. It stands with one foot sunk in the mud above a chamber and waits for the shed barbels to quiver as the Ledger Heron's bill lands, then spears down through the soft roof at exactly that spot. Because it works only by touch through the mud, its legs have grown a sheath of fine bristles that read each tremor like a stylus on a record, and its eyes have shrunk to dull pinpricks set far back on its head. The Stylus Worm, which feeds only on ground trodden by a pattern of stabs, spirals up around these bristled legs as the heron stands, and etches a faint groove on each shank, pale and wound tight like a threaded screw.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Screw Egret** (*Bubulcus helicoides*). It trails the Barbel Heron across the flats and probes the pale spiral grooves the Stylus Worm has etched into the heron's shanks, working its bill in with a slow clockwise twist as a cork is drawn, and it feeds on the salt-bloom that crystallizes in each groove. Because it only ever turns one way, its neck has grown a corkscrew curve and its skull sits cocked a quarter turn off its shoulders, so it walks the mud with its eye lowered sideways to the thread. The Thread Mussel, which closes its valves only against a spiral motion passing overhead, clamps shut as the egret's twisting bill goes by and leaves a ring of tight, pearl-lipped shells along the egret's path.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Pearl-Lip Whelk** (*Nucella margaritata*). It crawls the ring of clamped Thread Mussels the egret leaves behind and bores a neat round hole through each shell with its rasping tongue. It feeds on the soft flesh through the hole, and the pearl lip of the mussel guides the drill straight as a ruled circle. Because it cannot work on a shell that is open, the whelk waits for the water to leave the flats and the mussels to stay clenched, and its own shell has thickened into a heavy, ridged cone that holds the damp for days. The Drill Sparrow, which nests only in perfectly round holes, tucks its eggs into the emptied mussel shells and sits with its tail poking out through each borehole like a cork.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Cork Sparrow** (*Passer obturans*). It sits in each emptied mussel shell with its tail wedged through the borehole, and the seal is so snug that the tide, when it returns, flows over the shell without wetting the eggs, while the tail alone is bathed in brine. Because the tail is soaked every day, its feathers have fused into a stiff, smooth plug of keratin, and a sparrow that molts leaves the plug behind in the hole like a stopper in a bottle. The Bottle Bee, which seals its brood cells only in narrow-necked hollows that are already corked, hollows out these discarded plugs and lays its eggs in the core.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Core Wasp** (*Sceliphron nucleatus*). It hunts the Bottle Bee's plugged cells by the faint warmth of the brood within, and it drives a fine borer down the length of each keratin stopper until it reaches the core. There it lays a single egg beside the bee's larva, so the two grow up together in one hollow, the wasp grub slowly drinking the bee grub's honey-paste. Because the borer must pass through hard, glassy keratin again and again, the wasp's jaws have grown a tip of dark, diamond-hard enamel, and it carries a faint smell of burnt horn. The Horn Vole, which tunnels only toward the smell of scorched keratin and gnaws whatever it finds at the end, follows these wasps back along the roots to the shells where they nest.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Horn Vole** (*Microtus keratophagus*). It follows the scent of burnt horn along the roots and tunnels beneath each Core Wasp nest, gnawing upward through the floor until it breaks into the cell, and because it works only toward that smell, its tunnels run in a single rising line that never branches or wanders. Its incisors have grown long and chisel-flat, stained dark brown by the enamel dust it chews, and the same dust lines its cheeks so thickly that its whole face smells of the wasps it hunts. The Scent Snipe, which probes the mud for any burrow mouth that breathes out a smell of burning, stabs its bill down each vole tunnel as the vole leaves and has begun to drive the voles up out of the ground at the marsh edge in a scattering run.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Scatter Pipit** (*Anthus dispersus*). It follows the Scent Snipe's flushed voles across the marsh edge and takes the small beetles and flies that leap up from the grass at the vole's passing, snapping at each one in mid-air. Because the voles break in all directions at once, the pipit has grown a wide, fan-shaped tail it spreads and snaps shut in a quick flick to turn on the spot, and its legs have gone long and loose like a runner's. Each flick of that tail kicks a puff of dry grit across the turf, and the Grit Lark, which nests only in a scrape of finely sifted dust, gathers the settling puffs into a shallow cup and lays a single speckled egg in the middle.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Speckle Rail** (*Porzana variegata*). It creeps through the cordgrass beside the Grit Lark's dust-cup and takes only eggs whose speckling matches the pattern of the grit around them, ignoring any that stand out. Because the lark's egg is laid in the cup's very centre, the rail must step across the whole bed of sifted dust to reach it, and it has grown broad, webless toes that spread like snowshoes and leave no mark in the powder. Its own feathers have taken on a dusting of the same fine grit, and the Dust Bathing Quail, which can only wash in a hollow already shaped by another bird's body, lies down in the rail's faint, toe-less hollows at noon and fluffs the powder into the air in tall pale columns.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Column Swift** (*Chaetura pulverivaga*). It hunts only inside the pale columns of dust the Dust Bathing Quail throws up at noon, climbing each one in a tight spiral and snatching the gnats that rise with the powder. Because the dust stays aloft for just a few breaths, the swift has grown a stiff, flattened tail like a prop, which it jams against the settling grains to hold its place, and its feathers are so thickly coated that it flies as a dull, pale blur. The Chalk Lizard, which feeds on any bird that wears the color of the ground and lies unmoving on sun-bleached stones, waits at the foot of each column and takes the swifts as they drop out of the dust, exhausted, still wearing it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Chalk Lizard** (*Aporosaura calcaria*). It lies on sun-bleached stones at the foot of each dust column and takes the exhausted Column Swifts as they drop out, and because it swallows birds still caked in powder, its throat and belly have whitened to a hard, flaking crust that it sheds each evening in a single curled sheet. It lifts alternate feet off the hot stone in a slow, rocking dance, and the shed sheets, light and brittle as eggshell, slide down into the gullies between the rocks. The Sheet Bat, which roosts only beneath thin, curved plates that muffle the wind, hangs from the lizard's abandoned skins in the gullies and sleeps with its wings wrapped round its body like a rolled page.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Page Moth** (*Bombyx foliaris*). It feeds on the fine film of oil the Sheet Bat leaves along the inner curve of each shed lizard skin, and it settles on the rolled wings of the sleeping bat in tidy rows, folding its own wings flat so that the bat seems to wear a leaf of small print. Because the bat sleeps through the hottest hours without stirring, the moth has grown a faint ruled pattern of dark lines across its forewings, and a roost viewed from below reads like a ledger of pale columns. The Ledger Heron, which has wandered up from the flats at the end of a long dry spell and stands among the gullies in confusion, takes the rows for its own tally, and for the first time in its life strikes at an interval that is not prime.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Composite Stork** (*Ciconia numerosa*). It arrives in the gullies a day behind the Ledger Heron, and it feeds only on creatures that have just broken a long habit, so it stands patiently at the edge of the roost until a mistimed strike sends a startled lizard or bat scrambling across the stones. Because it waits so often in the shade of the shed skins, its long beak has grown a pale ruled stripe along each side, and it carries a thick, sagging throat-wattle that fills with the grit it swallows by accident. The Wattle Gecko, which roosts only in loose folds of skin that swing when the host walks, hangs inside the stork's wattle and fattens on the grit-borne mites, clicking its tail against the sagging skin with every stride.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Click Pipit** (*Anthus crepitans*). It follows the Composite Stork across the gullies and listens for the Wattle Gecko's tail striking the sagging skin, and it answers each click with a single sharp note, so that a walking stork is trailed by a bright, steady tapping like a stick run along a fence. Because it must keep pace with a long-legged bird, the pipit has grown a pair of tall, spindly legs and a habit of running in short bursts and then stopping dead, with its head cocked toward the throat above. The Fence Spider, which spins only along lines of regular tapping and takes any vibration for the edge of a post, strings its web between the pipit's legs as it pauses, and the bird must now step out of the silk at every halt.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Stirrup Mite** (*Trombidium retinaculum*). It lives in the sticky threads the Fence Spider strings between the Click Pipit's legs, and each time the pipit steps free it hooks a pair of forelegs over the torn strand and rides it up the shank like a foot in a stirrup. Because the thread snaps back at the end of every step, the mite has grown a springy, coiled joint at the base of each leg that stores the recoil, and it flings itself a full pipit's-length ahead on each snap. The Leap Plover, which chases any small speck that jumps in a straight line across open ground, has taken to running down the track of these flights and stopping short at each landing spot.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Landing Beetle** (*Carabus destinator*). It lives in the shallow dimples the Leap Plover stamps at each stop, and it feeds on the crushed remains of the Stirrup Mites that the plover's sudden halts grind into the dust. Because every dimple is pressed by the same hard, three-toed heel, the beetle has grown a hollow in its shell the shape of that heel, and it sits in each pit as a stone sits in its socket. Its back is the one place on the flats where rain pools in a perfect small oval, and the Mirror Dragonfly, which hovers only over still water no bigger than a thumbnail, hangs in the air above each beetle and watches its own reflection for hours.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Mirror Dragonfly** (*Anax speculator*). It hangs above the rain-filled hollow on a Landing Beetle's back and holds its position by keeping its reflection exactly centred in the oval, so that a beetle which shifts even a little drags the dragonfly sideways through the air in the same direction. Because it hovers for hours on a surface that never stills, its wings have grown a thin silvered coating on the underside that flashes in time with each correction, and a dragonfly on station looks like a bright coin being slowly tilted. The Coin Finch, which collects any small disc that glints and carries it to a nest of stacked rims, takes these flashes for lost silver, and flies down to pick the dragonflies off the beetles' backs one at a time.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Coin Finch** (*Fringilla nummularia*). It carries each captured dragonfly to a nest of stacked rims, tucking the silvered wings flat against the wall like coins set on edge, and its beak has grown a small pincer-shaped notch that grips a wing by its rim without bending it. Because the wings hold their glint for only a day, the finch keeps its nest turning like a market stall, discarding dull wings off the rim of the nest as it adds bright ones, and the discards fall in a slow glittering rain onto the ground below. The Tarnish Beetle, which feeds only on metal gone dull and lays its eggs in anything that has lost its shine, gathers beneath the nest and burrows into each fallen wing.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Tarnish Beetle** (*Chrysina obscura*). It burrows into each fallen wing from the dull edge inward and feeds on the last film of silver, so a wing that lands bright is hollowed to a grey lace within a night, and the beetle emerges from it coated in a fine black bloom that it cannot brush off. Because it must wait for the shine to go before it can eat, the beetle has grown a pair of long, sensitive feelers that test the surface of every wing by touch and recoil from any glint, and it crouches in the shade of the nest's overhang while the bright ones fall past. The Soot Warbler, which sings only when something dark is crawling beneath it on pale ground, perches above the blackened beetles and answers each one's slow passage with a low, sooty phrase that darkens as the beetle nears the edge of the stones.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Edge Wren** (*Troglodytes marginalis*). It nests in the last crevice before the flat stones give way to marsh and sings only when a Soot Warbler's phrase has fallen to its lowest note, answering with a thin bright figure that climbs just as the darkness peaks. Because it must listen through the whole descent before it sings, the wren has grown tall, cupped ear-tufts that fold shut during the warbler's louder phrases and spring open at the final dip, and it perches with its head tipped over the stone's edge like a person at a rail. Seeds that drop from its crevice sprout into the Lip Sedge, which grows only along the exact boundary between stone and mud, and the Marsh Rail, which has long walked the cordgrass, now picks its way along this thin green line at dusk.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Lip Sedge Rail** (*Rallus marginatus*). It walks the thin green line of Lip Sedge at dusk with one foot on stone and one in mud, and because the sedge grows only along that exact boundary, its stride has lopsided over generations: the stone-side leg has grown short and hard-soled, the mud-side leg long and splayed, so it moves in a steady, tilting roll like a boat on a slow swell. It eats the seed-heads of the sedge by drawing each stem across its bill, and the husks it strips fall into a narrow windrow along the boundary, pale as a chalk line ruled by a careful hand. The Chalk-Line Beetle, which can only travel along a straight edge of pale husk, marches single file down that windrow, and its columns now mark the exact border of the marsh from one end of the flats to the other.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Border Heron** (*Ardea limitans*). It stalks the flats beside the Chalk-Line Beetles' column and treats the pale line as a wall, so it fishes only on the marsh side, standing at the exact point where the beetles' file turns to follow a bend. Because the line is the one fixed thing on a shore that tides rework twice a day, its legs have grown marked in rings of dark and pale at the height of each tide, and a heron's age can be read from the number of rings it has worn above the water. The Tide-Mark Barnacle, which settles only on a surface already banded by waterlines, cements itself in rows to these ringed shanks and opens its plates in time with the rising of each ring.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Shank Limpet** (*Patella annularis*). It grazes the film of algae that blooms between the Tide-Mark Barnacle's open plates, and it travels only upward along a Border Heron's leg, one ring above the last, as the water climbs, then clamps down and rests through the ebb. Because the heron stands so still while the tide rises, the limpet's shell has grown a flattened, tilted rim that sits flush against the curve of a shank, and its foot leaves a thin glassy trail that hardens into a spiral glaze around the leg. The Glaze Kingfisher, which dives only at objects that flash with a wet, even gloss, mistakes the spiralled legs for stems of ice and plunges at them from the reeds, striking the heron's shank with the flat of its bill.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: **The Shank Heron's Tapper, the Flat-Bill Kingfisher** (*Alcedo plana*). It dives at the glazed shanks and strikes with the flat of its bill, never the point, so its beak has broadened into a stiff paddle and each failed dive leaves a clean bright ring of tapped glaze on the leg. Because it hits the same spiral hundreds of times a season, the glaze cracks along the strike line in a fine pattern of splinters, and the heron, feeling the faint knock, lifts that foot slowly and sets it down again an inch to the side. The Splinter Mayfly, which emerges only from cracked, glassy surfaces and lives a single hour, rises from the fractures in clouds just as the heron shifts, and the whole flat shimmers briefly with their rising.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: **The Shimmer Swallow** (*Hirundo micans*). It skims the flats in the hour the Splinter Mayflies rise and feeds only on that single cloud, flying low through the shimmer with its mouth held open and its eyes closed against the glitter. Because the mayflies live just sixty minutes, the swallow has grown a short, hard-feathered body built for a single frantic sweep of the marsh, and it fattens so quickly in that hour that its breast feathers lift and separate, showing a bare pink band along the keel. The Keel Crab, which tracks any warm bare patch moving low over the mud, scuttles along beneath the swallow's passing and rears up to nip at the band as it flashes overhead.
